newsitem.title: MALI: Mali opposition rejects poll, denounces violence.
newsitem.headline: Mali opposition rejects poll, denounces violence.

text.p: Mali's radical opposition on Monday pronounced the West African nation's rerun parliamentary election a failure and accused President Alpha Oumar Konare of resorting to violence to hang onto power.

An 18-party opposition alliance, which boycotted and disrupted Sunday's election, repeated a call for Konare and his government to stand down. It said two people killed in clashes in the town of San were its militants.
This year's elections have been a far-cry from Mali's widely praised 1992 democratic transition.
"These elections are a disgrace for the ruling ADEMA party because the turnout cannot be more than 10 percent," the opposition alliance said as votes were counted.

"Savage repression, during which live ammunition was fired, private property destroyed and injury inflicted, was employed on July 20 1997 to make possible Alpha Oumar Konare's second civilian coup," it added.
Malian newspapers headlined "The electoral fiasco", "Morning of opposition excesses and harassment" or "Spiral of violence".
Mali was one of the stars of Africa's 1990s democracy movement, drawing widespread praise from its 1992 transition from Moussa Traore's dictatorship to multi-party democracy.
The constitutional court, citing irregularities, scrapped a chaotic April 13 parliamentary election which kicked off the former French colony's second multi-party national elections.

The opposition wanted the whole election timetable revised but Konare, a historian first elected in 1992, pressed ahead with only minor modifications. He won a new five-year term on May 11 in an election which the main opposition also boycotted.
The radical opposition, which includes Moussa Troare supporters, has stood by its demand throughout.
Almost 600 candidates from Konare's Alliance for Democracy in Mali (ADEMA), 18 other parties and 13 independent lists contested the 147 seats at stake in the national assembly.
Witnesses and polling officials said turnout in Sunday's polling appeared to be low.

State television said the two people were killed in the opposition stronghold of San, east of the capital Bamako. Witnesses reported armed attacks in San on polling stations, some of which were ransacked and set on fire.
Prime Minister Ibrahim Keita said those responsible for vandalism or violence would be prosecuted.
Polling in Bamako was peaceful but state radio and witnesses reported that polling stations and cars were ransacked or set ablaze in Segou, Kolokani and Sikasso.
Turnout in the scrapped April 13 poll was around 30 percent. On May 11, when Konare was re-elected, it was just 28 percent.

Mali, arid, impoverished and mainly Moslem, won independence from France in 1960. It takes its name from a pre-colonial African empire that built its power on gold and flourished when Europe was in the Middle Ages.
Gold remains a major source of foreign exchange.
The opposition alliance includes supporters of Traore, who remains in detention, and of independence leader Modibo Keita, who ruled Mali as a pro-Soviet one-party socialist state.
Final results, to be ratified by the constitutional court, were expected by Wednesday. A run-off will be held on August 3.
